extra_misconceptions.fact: Standard eyeglasses lack side shields and shatter-resistant lenses, so woodworkers must wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses over them.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Everyday prescription eyeglasses provide enough impact protection to replace ANSI-rated safety goggles in a woodshop.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Dull blades require excessive pushing force and slip off the wood grain easily, causing severe lacerations when the tool skids.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Dull chisels and hand planes are safer for beginners because their rounded edges are less likely to cut skin.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Fine wood dust from oak, walnut, and western red cedar is a known respiratory sensitizer and carcinogen requiring an N95 dust mask.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sawdust from kiln-dried domestic hardwoods is harmless nuisance dust that only requires sweeping up after a project.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rubbing embeds sharp wood fibers into the cornea; flush the open eye gently with clean water and cover it if irritation persists.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Rubbing a gritty woodshop eye injury helps flush the sawdust particle toward the tear duct for easy removal.

extra_socratic_questions: Why is it dangerous to wear woven work gloves when operating a stationary drill press or lathe?
What happens to a crumpled rag soaked in boiled linseed oil if you toss it into a closed trash bin?
Where should a Scout position both hands relative to the chisel bevel before striking the handle with a mallet?
Under what condition does a deep wood splinter require professional medical extraction rather than tweezers?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Hardwood and softwood are botanical terms based on enclosed seeds versus naked cones; balsa is a deciduous broadleaf hardwood.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Hardwoods are always physically harder and denser than softwoods, which is why balsa is classified as a softwood.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Kiln drying and planing all four faces reduce a nominal two-by-four board to an actual finished size of 1.5 by 3.5 inches.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Nominal two-by-four dimensional lumber measures a full two inches thick by four inches wide at the hardware store.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Kiln drying lowers moisture content to roughly 6 to 8 percent, and cured wood still expands and contracts with seasonal humidity.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Kiln drying removes 100 percent of the moisture from green timber so the boards can never warp or shrink again.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Tightly stacked green boards trap moisture and rot; narrow wooden stickers must space each layer so air circulates evenly.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Stacking freshly milled green planks flat on top of each other keeps them straight while they air-dry in a shed.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the width and flatness of a plain-sawn board if you build furniture before the wood finishes seasoning?
Which physical indicator on a board's end grain distinguishes quartersawn oak from plain-sawn oak?
What measurement confirms that a nominal two-by-four stud has been surfaced on all four sides at the lumber mill?
Why does structural grading for softwood framing lumber use different defect standards than FAS hardwood grading?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A chisel back must remain dead flat to guide paring cuts accurately, so only the angled bevel side is ground and honed.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sharpening both sides of a bench chisel like a kitchen knife creates a stronger, more symmetrical cutting edge.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Heavy grinding pressure overheats the thin steel edge, turning it blue and ruining the temper so it can no longer hold an edge.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Pressing down with maximum weight on a dry high-speed bench grinder removes nicks from a plane iron much faster.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Silicone contaminates bare wood and causes fish-eye craters in varnish and stain; protect cast iron with wax or mineral oil instead.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Spraying silicone lubricant on cast-iron hand tools is better than camellia oil or paste wax because it never dries.

extra_misconceptions.fact: An unremoved wire burr folds over or snaps off on the first stroke, leaving a ragged, dull edge that tears the wood fibers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Leaving the wire burr attached after honing on a coarse oilstone makes a plane iron bite into hardwood more cleanly.

extra_socratic_questions: Which physical indicator along the flat back of a chisel confirms you have honed all the way to the cutting apex?
What happens to a bench plane's cutting action if you store it resting flat on its sole with the iron extended?
Why is it dangerous to lift a chisel handle while lapping the flat back of the blade on a finishing stone?
Under what condition does a bevel edge require re-grinding at 25 degrees before honing a 30-degree micro-bevel?

extra_misconceptions.fact: The saw blade kerf removes roughly one-sixteenth of an inch of wood, so you must cut on the waste side and leave the line visible.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sawing directly down the center of your pencil layout line guarantees that every board matches the exact plan length.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Rip teeth are filed flat like tiny chisels to pare along the grain, while crosscut teeth are beveled like knives to sever fibers.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A rip saw and a crosscut saw have identical teeth, except a rip saw has more teeth per inch for smoother cuts.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Planing uphill into rising grain lifts and splits the fibers ahead of the blade, causing chip-out; always plane with the grain.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Planing against rising wood grain produces a smoother board because the plane iron lifts and shears the fibers cleanly.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Choking up near the hammer head sacrifices lever momentum and wrist snap; grip near the end of the handle for accurate strikes.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Gripping a claw hammer right behind the steel head gives you maximum striking power and control when driving nails.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to the exit face of a board if you drill all the way through with an auger bit in a single pass?
Which physical indicator tells you whether to reach for a crosscut handsaw or a rip handsaw before making a cut?
Where should a Scout position the saw kerf relative to the layout line so the finished board matches the drawing?
What measurement confirms that a hand-planed reference edge is truly ninety degrees to the reference face?

extra_misconceptions.fact: A board foot is a volume measurement equal to 144 cubic inches, such as a board one inch thick by twelve inches wide by twelve inches long.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: One board foot of lumber equals any board that measures twelve inches long regardless of its width or thickness.

extra_misconceptions.fact: A complete bill of materials must include rough stock allowances for squaring and kerf waste, plus fasteners, glue, and finish.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A bill of materials only needs to list the exact net dimensions of the finished wooden parts shown on the drawing.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Small thickness variations accumulate during milling, so taking relative measurements directly from the assembled frame ensures tight fits.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Measuring every joint from the original paper plan during final assembly is more accurate than measuring the actual project.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Surface preparation and multi-coat finishing often consume a third of total build hours and a major share of the materials budget.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Sanding and applying stain or polyurethane takes only a few minutes and does not need to be tracked in the project log.

extra_socratic_questions: What measurement confirms how many board feet of four-quarter hardwood you are buying at a specialty lumberyard?
Why is it dangerous to lay out and cut every project piece at once before checking the fit of your main subassemblies?
Under what condition does a working drawing require top, front, and side orthographic views instead of a single sketch?
What happens to your material budget if your bill of materials omits waste allowance for defects and saw kerfs?

extra_misconceptions.fact: End grain absorbs glue poorly, making plain miter joints weak unless reinforced with splines, dowels, biscuits, or keys.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A forty-five-degree miter joint glued end-to-end is one of the strongest structural corner joints for heavy cabinet frames.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Water-based wood glue swells wood fibers and hydraulic pressure from a too-tight tenon will split the mortise walls along the grain.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: A tenon that requires heavy pounding with a mallet to enter the mortise during a dry fit will make the strongest joint.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Excessive clamping pressure squeezes almost all adhesive out of the joint interface, creating a weak, glue-starved bond.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cranking bar clamps as tightly as possible squeezes glue deep into the wood pores and increases joint strength.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Even slight angle or center drift causes dowel joints to bind or step out of alignment, so a self-centering doweling jig is essential.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Drilling dowel holes freehand with a power drill is accurate enough to align mating cabinet boards flush on both faces.

extra_socratic_questions: What happens to a solid wood cabinet door if you glue the center panel tightly into all four sides of the frame grooves?
Which physical indicator during a dry clamp-up confirms that a cabinet carcass is free of twist and truly square?
Why is it dangerous to force an oversized hardwood tenon into a tight mortise with heavy hammer blows during glue-up?
Where should a Scout position the marking gauge fence when scribing both the mortise walls and the mating tenon cheeks?

extra_misconceptions.fact: Cabinetmakers build casework and furniture using stationary shop machinery, while finish carpenters install trim and millwork on job sites.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Cabinetmakers and finish carpenters perform the exact same job and work in the same locations throughout the week.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Shop automation speeds up repetitive part cutting, but cabinetmakers still rely on hand planes, chisels, and scribing for custom fitting.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Modern CNC routers and automated saws have eliminated the need for hand-tool and layout skills in professional cabinetry.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Registered carpentry apprenticeships use an earn-while-you-learn model that combines paid on-the-job hours with classroom instruction.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Carpentry apprentices must pay high tuition out of pocket for four years before they are allowed to work for pay.

extra_misconceptions.fact: Framed walls are rarely plumb or ninety degrees, so finish carpenters must cope inside corners and scribe trim to fit uneven surfaces.
extra_misconceptions.misconception: Finish carpenters can cut baseboard and crown molding to exact blueprint measurements without checking the drywall corners.
